report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that soursop (also called graviola or *Annona muricata*) cures cancer in humans is **not supported by reliable clinical evidence**.

**What supports the idea:** Laboratory studies have found that soursop extracts and compounds can damage or slow growth of some cancer-cell lines. This is hypothesis-generating research, not evidence of a cure: substances that kill isolated cells often fail in people because of dosing, absorption, toxicity, and tumor biology. Cancer Research UK reports that these results have **not been tested in humans** as a cancer treatment. [Cancer Research UK](https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/treatment/complementary-alternative-therapies/individual-therapies/graviola)

**What is missing:** There are no high-quality, completed human trials showing soursop cures cancer, improves survival, shrinks tumors, or can safely replace established treatment. A scientific review similarly says clinical trials of *A. muricata*’s potential have been markedly neglected. [PubMed Central review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4519917/)

**Safety:** “Natural” does not mean harmless. Memorial Sloan Kettering notes laboratory and animal concerns involving neurologic toxicity resembling Parkinson-like movement disorders/myeloneuropathy with graviola compounds or long-term juice intake. [Memorial Sloan Kettering](https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/graviola)

**Practical takeaway:** Eating soursop as an occasional food is different from taking concentrated leaf, seed, tea, or supplement products. Do not use these products instead of cancer care or delay proven treatment; discuss any supplement with the oncology team, especially because interactions and product doses vary. Promotional cure claims are based largely on laboratory findings and anecdotes, not human outcomes. [Cancer Research UK](https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/treatment/complementary-alternative-therapies/individual-therapies/graviola)
